question.value: What is the occurrence rate and what are the properties of debris discs around F stars in the 23 Myr-old beta Pic moving group compared to other young moving groups and older field stars, and what explains the rapid decay in fractional luminosity?

evidence.quote: Only 20% of old field stars have detectable debris discs, leaving open the question of what disc, if any, is present around the remaining 80%.
This paper considers the population of F stars in the 23 Myr-old BPMG where we find that 9/12 targets possess discs.
This is higher than the $20\%$ seen for Gyr-old stars (cite: su-et-al-2006; marshall-et-al-2016; sibthorpe-et-al-2018) leading to the question why we get such a high frequency.

assumptions.value: Dust acts like blackbodies in equilibrium with stellar radiation for R_BB; parameter values follow a normal distribution for confidence levels

After producing a model image, we Fourier Transform it and sample the model visibility function at the same *u-v* locations as the data using the GALARIO software package (cite: tazzari-et-al-2018).

This process is then used to fit the model to the data through a Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) implemented using the EMCEE v3 software package (cite: foreman-mackey-et-al-2013; foreman-mackey-et-al-2019).

In addition to the model parameters entering the equation describing the density distribution, we fit for RA and Dec offsets of the belt’s geometric center from the phase center of the observations, and for a weight rescaling factor to account for the inaccurate data weights (and hence uncertainties) typically delivered by ALMA (cite: marino-et-al-2018; matra-et-al-2019b).

claims.hypothesis: The debris disc incidence rate around F stars in young (<100 Myr) moving groups (BPMG and 45 Myr group) is higher than around older field F stars (DEBRIS sample).
claims.experiment: Fit SEDs of F stars in BPMG (12 stars), 45 Myr group (29 stars), 150 Myr group (13 stars), and DEBRIS field sample (92 stars), and compare detection rates using Fisher's exact test.
claims.result: Disc detection rates are 75% (9/12) in BPMG, 37.9% (11/29) in the 45 Myr group, 15.4% (2/13) in the 150 Myr group, and 22.8% (21/92) in DEBRIS; Fisher's exact test gives p = 7.9x10^-4 (BPMG vs DEBRIS) and p = 0.013 (45 Myr vs DEBRIS), while BPMG vs 45 Myr gives p = 0.45.
claims.finding: Young moving groups (<100 Myr) have a statistically significantly higher debris disc detection rate around F stars than old field stars, and comparable rates to each other.

evidence.quote: We found that for the BPMG the probability $p = 7.9\times 10^{-4}$, for the 45 Myr group $p = 0.013$ and for the 150 Myr group $p = 0.68$.

Therefore, we can say that for BPMG and the 45 Myr group the detection rates are not similar to that of the DEBRIS sample. In addition, we tested whether the rates of the BPMG and the 45 Myr group are different from each other and found $p = 0.45$.

claims.hypothesis: The ratio of spatially resolved sub-mm disc radius to blackbody radius decreases with stellar luminosity following the same steep trend (A = 6.49, B = -0.37) previously derived from Herschel FIR images.
claims.experiment: Measure sub-mm radii for 4 BPMG F-star discs with ALMA visibility modelling (plus 1 SPHERE disc), combine with the Matrà et al. (2018) ALMA sample, and fit R_disc/R_BB = A*(L/L_sun)^B.
claims.result: TheBPMG F-star discs have ratios between 1.6 and 3.4, yielding a best-fit trend with A = 2.92 +/- 0.50 and B = -0.13 +/- 0.07.
claims.finding: The ALMA-derived radius ratio shows a weaker decrease with stellar luminosity than the Herschel-based relation because lower-luminosity F-star discs have smaller ratios than predicted by the Herschel trend.

evidence.loc: Ratio of spatially resolved disc radius to blackbody radius
evidence.quote: For our sample of F stars the values of this ratio lie between 1.6 and 3.4 where the system with the lowest stellar luminosity (HD 160305) possesses the highest value. Including the ALMA-sample of (cite: matra-et-al-2018) and fitting a trend of the form in eq. [\[eq:trueradius\]](#eq:trueradius) for how the ratio depends on stellar luminosity we infer a slight decrease of the ratio with stellar luminosity finding parameter values of $A = 2.92\pm0.50$ and $B=-0.13\pm0.07$.

Since ALMA has a higher spatial resolution than *Herschel* we inferred the sub-mm disc to blackbody radius ratio - stellar luminosity relation from a sample of ALMA data (cite: matra-et-al-2018). The resulting relation shows a weaker decrease of the radius ratio with increasing stellar luminosity.

claims.hypothesis: Debris discs in the BPMG are smaller than those around older field F stars in the DEBRIS sample.
claims.experiment: Compare blackbody radius distributions and spatially resolved (ALMA, Herschel, SPHERE) disc radii between the BPMG, 45 Myr, 150 Myr, and DEBRIS samples.
claims.result: BPMG resolved disc radii lie between 45 and 94 au whereas 6/9 resolved DEBRIS discs lie at ~100-150 au, and only DEBRIS has R_BB > 100 au discs (4/92), though detecting zero >100 au discs in 12 BPMG stars has a 41.3% probability under the DEBRIS rate.
claims.finding: BPMG discs tend to be smaller than those around field stars, but the difference is not statistically significant due to small sample sizes and potential Herschel resolution biases.

evidence.quote: The BPMG discs tend to be smaller than those around field stars. However, this difference is not statistically significant due to the small number of targets.
For example, the probability of detecting one or more $>100$ au disc in the BPMG sample of only twelve stars would be 41.3% if their incidence rate was the same as that of the DEBRIS sample of 4/92.

claims.hypothesis: Standard steady-state collisional evolution (f_d proportional to t^-1) of the BPMG disc population can explain the lower detection rate observed in the older DEBRIS field star sample.
claims.experiment: Simulate 100,000 artificial 92-star samples drawn from the BPMG sample, evolve their fractional luminosities to random field-star ages using f_d(t) = f_d(t_0)*(t/t_0)^alpha, and apply the DEBRIS completeness map.
claims.result: Standard collisional evolution (t_0 = 23 Myr, alpha = -1) predicts a DEBRIS detection rate of 41 +/- 10%, incompatible with the observed 22.8 +6.2/-4.9%; matching DEBRIS requires faster depletion equivalent to alpha = -2 (a drop of two orders of magnitude within 100 Myr), which can be caused by embedded 20-170 M_earth planets (though different birth environments cannot be ruled out).
claims.finding: Simple steady-state collisional evolution alone cannot link the BPMG and DEBRIS populations; rapid depletion within the first 100 Myr (e.g. by Neptune-mass planets) or different star-forming environments is required.

evidence.quote: The dashed red line in Fig. [10](#fig:Evolution) shows that in this case the DEBRIS sample should have a detection rate of $41\pm10\,\%$ following Poisson statistics with a 95% confidence level. This is incompatible with the observed detection rate of $22.8^{+6.2}_{-4.9}$% for the DEBRIS sample.

The other explanation that is compatible with the assumption of similar disc populations in the BPMG and DEBRIS samples is that the evolution is faster than $t^{-1}$. The dash-dotted orange line in Fig. [10](#fig:Evolution) shows that $t^{-2}$ is in agreement with this hypothesis.

We attribute this depletion to embedded planets which would be around 170 $M_\text{earth}$ to cause a depletion on the appropriate timescale. However, we cannot rule out that different birth environments of nearby young clusters result in brighter debris discs than the progenitors of field stars which likely formed in a more dense environment.

why_this_data.value: Young nearby moving groups (<100 Myr) like BPMG have discs at their brightest and are coeval; F-type stars offer the best compromise between high stellar luminosity (maximizing disc detection) and a reasonably large sample size; sub-mm ALMA observations trace mm-sized grains that stay close to the parent planetesimal belt.

evidence.quote: The best compromise between a high stellar luminosity and a reasonably large number of targets within the same moving group is given by F-type stars.

Hence, the disc size inferred in sub-mm observations is the best tracer of the location of a system’s planetesimal belt, which might differ from the radial extent seen in near-infrared scattered light.

why_this_method.value: Re-analysing archival ALMA visibilities with a uniform 3D Gaussian model (RADMC-3D + GALARIO + EMCEE) and Herschel images with a uniform PSF-convolved model ensures homogeneous radius measurements across the sample; completeness maps in f_d vs R_BB space remove distance and sensitivity biases when comparing samples.

evidence.quote: Three of the analysed datasets have already been presented in literature work (cite: macgregor-et-al-2019; perez-et-al-2019; kral-et-al-2020), but are re-analysed here to maintain consistency across the sample.
Plotting detection rate versus age can be misleading, since different surveys reach different sensitivities to discs, for example due to the different distance of the stars in their samples.

alternatives_considered_or_rejected.value: 2D power-law radial surface density model with a gap for HD 15115 (MacGregor et al. 2019): not needed when using a 3D Gaussian radial and vertical density model.

evidence.quote: Our results do not show evidence for a gap in the disc, which may be because of the different parameterisations of the two models; (cite: macgregor-et-al-2019) assumes a 2D disc model using a power law for the radial surface density distribution and an infinitesimally small vertical scale height, whereas our disc model assumes Gaussian radial and vertical density distributions (the latter was found to be marginally resolved in our analysis).

alternatives_considered_or_rejected.value: Delayed stirring (t_0 ~ 2 Myr, waiting 21 Myr to ignite collisional cascade): rejected as unrealistic because protoplanetary discs dissipate in a few Myr and discs at different radii have different evolution timescales.

evidence.quote: While delayed stirring is expected in some models (cite: kenyon-bromley-2008), this explanation would require all discs to wait 21 Myr before being ignited, whereas all discs are located at different radii and so should have different evolution timescales.

alternatives_considered_or_rejected.value: Gas drag or evolving small-grain size distribution causing rapid luminosity drop: rejected because no significant gas is present and SED models show no evidence for changing s_min or q.

evidence.quote: However, there is no evidence for a change in small dust properties in the SED models’ $s_\text{min}$ or $q$, and there is not significant gas in these systems.

alternatives_considered_or_rejected.value: Planetesimal depletion via stellar flare heating or YORP radiation forces: rejected for the bulk sample because most BPMG discs lie at ~80 au where these effects are negligible.

evidence.quote: However, the majority of the discs in the BPMG lie too far out ($\sim80$ au) for this to be important.

However, the relatively slow evolution of Solar system asteroids (cite: durech-et-al-2018) suggests that this radiation effect might be negligible, since it should be weaker for planetesimals at several tens of au.

alternatives_considered_or_rejected.value: Two-population scenario (swept-up primordial dust ring + faint outer Kuiper-belt analogue): considered unlikely on its own because outer DEBRIS-like belts are not detected and the inner belts still require rapid non-collisional depletion.

evidence.quote: However, while the two-population scenario is not impossible, we would still need to invoke a rapid depletion as proposed in the first scenario (§ [7.1](#sec:samepopulation)).

limitations_admitted.value: Small number of targets in the BPMG (12 stars) and small number of spatially resolved discs limit the statistical significance of radius distribution comparisons.

evidence.quote: However, this difference is not statistically significant due to the small number of targets.

limitations_admitted.value: HD 173167 and several stars in the 45 Myr and 150 Myr moving groups lack far-infrared photometry beyond 22 um (or only have IRAS upper limits), preventing firm conclusions on cold disc presence for those stars.

evidence.quote: The star HD 173167 only possesses photometric data up to 22$\mu$m so that we cannot draw any conclusions about a possible far-infrared excess.
For several targets only data up to mid-infrared wavelengths (WISE22) are available or upper limits from IRAS at 25, 60 and 100$\mu$m, but no *Spitzer*/MIPS or other far-infrared data.

limitations_admitted.value: High ALMA upper limits for HD 14082A (<5.8 mJy) and HD 29391 (<3.5 mJy) due to the 14" phase-center offset (46% primary beam response) for HD 14082A and the small 0.2" beam for HD 29391.

evidence.quote: The high values for the upper limits are caused by the relatively small beam used for the observation of HD 29391 and the fact that HD 14082A is significantly offset from the phase center, increasing the already high RMS of that observation.

limitations_admitted.value: Visual inspection of CO J=3-2 in HD 181327 yielded a non-detection, and a full gas analysis optimising detection across excitation conditions was not performed.

evidence.quote: The non-detection could be consistent with the J=2-1 detection depending on excitation conditions, but a full gas analysis, including optimising detection, and considering the wide range of possible excitation conditions is needed to draw a definitive conclusion.

limitations_admitted.value: Minimum grain size s_min inferred for HD 15115 may be influenced by how the warm inner component was treated.

evidence.quote: However, the difference in $s_\text{min}$ of this disc to the others in the sample should be treated with caution, since the minimum grain size that we infer may be influenced by how we treated the warm component that is only present in this system.

limitations_admitted.value: Catastrophic disruption threshold Q_D* varies by an order of magnitude depending on material and velocity-scaling method, leading to large uncertainties in minimum planetesimal sizes and disc masses.

evidence.quote: Therefore, we emphasise that $Q_\text{D}^*$ strongly depends on the method applied and shows variations of one order of magnitude even for the same material.

referee_caveats_inferred: Inhomogeneous archival ALMA observations (Band 6 vs Band 7, beams from 0.2" to 1.8", RMS from 12 to 326 uJy/beam) across the 6 observed BPMG targets.

Comparison of resolved disc radii between BPMG and DEBRIS mixes ALMA sub-mm Gaussian peak radii (for most BPMG discs) with lower-resolution Herschel/PACS power-law midpoint radii (for 7/9 DEBRIS resolved discs).

There is a discrepancy between the text in Section 3.2/3.3 (reporting T_BB = 51 to 600 K and R_BB = 0.3 to 52 au, with HD 199143 at 600 K / 0.3 au and HD 29391 at R_BB = 9 +/- 2 au) and Table 3 (which lists T_bb = 1000 +/- 100 K and R_bb = 0.2 +/- 0.1 au for HD 199143, and R_bb = 18 +/- 5 au for HD 29391).

data_public_as_stated.value: ALMA and Herschel data are publicly available in their respective archives; underlying article data shared on request to the corresponding author.

evidence.quote: The data underlying this article will be shared on request to the corresponding author.
